Learning Objectives
Identify options for shoe modification and bracing and orthotic options for common foot and
ankle deformities and conditions.
Describe material properties and design rationale for common orthoses and lower extremity
braces.
Shoe Selection
Shoes may help reduce the risk of ulceration,1 stress fractures, and overuse injuries.
Goals: protecting the foot; relieving areas of excess pressure; reducing shock and shear; and
accommodating, stabilizing, and supporting deformities.2

Shoe Selection
Careful selection of cushioned and supportive shoes may help reduce the risk of
ulceration, stress fractures, and overuse injuries. Many off-the-shelf walking or running
shoes can be used as extra-depth shoes if the insole is removed. For more severe
deformities, extra-depth oxford-style shoes may need to be modified. For feet with
Charcot deformities or severe malalignment, custom-molded shoes may be necessary. In
general, flexible flatfeet require a firm medial arch support and a straight last, whereas a
more rigid cavus foot benefits from a shoe that offers cushioning and shock absorption3
(Table 1).
Table 1 Basic Shoe Components
Component
Description
Upper
Portion of the shoe enclosing the dorsum of the foot above the
insole; includes the toe box, vamp, and quarter.
Lower
Portion of the shoe plantar to the foot; includes the insole,
midsole, and outsole.
Toe box
Distal portion of the upper that provides space for the toes
Vamp
Midsection of the upper that covers the dorsum of the midfoot
Quarter
Posterior portion of the upper that covers the hindfoot
posteriorly and laterally; may have a reinforced area around the
heel known as the heel counter.

Shoe Modification
Many modifications can be made to shoes to off load painful foot and ankle deformities.
Stability can be improved via flares to correct or off load varus or valgus deformities. An
extended shank can reduce motion through painful, unstable, stiff, or arthritic joints.
Forward propulsion and off-loading of bony prominences can be improved with the use
of a rocker-bottom sole. Variations in placement or incline can be optimized to
redistribute forces away from pathologic segments of the foot. Caution should be
exercised in prescribing rocker-bottom soles for patients with impairments in sensation,
proprioception, or balance. Relasting is a versatile option for making custom
modifications to a shoe without substantially altering its aesthetics. Elevating, posting,
and increasing shock absorption can be performed via this modification to the midsole
or outsole2 (Table 2).
Table 2 Shoe Types and Modifications
Type
Description
In-depth shoe
Additional 0.25-inch to 0.375-inch depth to accommodate
deformity; often manufactured with factory insoles that can be
exchanged easily.
Custom shoe
May provide the best accommodation and protection because it
is fabricated from a positive model of a mold or from CT scan
Relasting
The customization of an off-the-shelf shoe to accommodate
deformity without sacrificing the normal appearance to the
casual observer; outsole is removed and a cut is made through
the remaining sole; material is added into the cut to fill the gap
and widen the shoe; a new outsole is applied.
Flare
A firm strip of material added as an outrigger to provide a wider
base of support on the shoe surface for increased stability

Shank
Steel or carbon composite embedded in the layers of the sole to
stiffen it from heel to toe; used to reduce bending in the shoe.
Rocker sole
Additional material added in the midsole to create a rocker to
allow the foot to roll over from heel strike to toe-off with reduced
bending; multiple types exist, but generally the apex of the rocker
is placed proximal to the area at which pressure relief is desired.

Insole placed within a shoe to provide cushioning, shock absorption, support and control, to

Custom versus prefabricated orthoses

Expensive, made from a mold or model of the patient’s foot
Allows for custom fit, increased longevity, and modification or adjustment

Prefabricated orthoses
Lower cost
Ease of use and off-the-shelf availability
Cannot accommodate substantial deformity
Types of custom foot orthoses
Accommodative: cushion and protect the foot through shock absorption and padding
Best for patients with minimal deformity and those who require preventive padding (ie,
metatarsalgia, fat pad loss)
Rigid: support or correct flexible deformities, low profile
Durable and offer support and control
Offer minimal cushioning, shock absorption, and protection; may cause skin breakdown if
foot deformity is present.
Best for patients with flexible deformities (ie, pes planovalgus)
Semirigid: support, control

Materials used for accommodative orthoses
Soft cross-linked polyethylene foams: heat moldable and very soft but compress quickly and
not as durable
Open-cell polyurethane foams: reduce shear and absorb shock
Polyethylene foams: better pressure distribution but rapidly lose thickness under load
compared with polyurethane foams6
Sponge rubber: varying densities; can maintain its shape and thickness under heavy loads.
Material for semi-rigid orthoses
Top layer: accommodative materials
Support/base
Ethylene vinyl acetates: last longer; structure holds up better than polyethylene foams.
Cork composites: good shock absorbers; do not compress quickly.
3D printing: ethylene vinyl acetates, polypropylene, carbon fiber
Materials for rigid orthoses
Made from carbon fiber composites or thermoplastic polyurethanes
Difficult to adjust after fabrication
Specific modifications to foot orthoses
Full-length, sulcus-length (to base of toes), three quarter-length (ends proximal to metatarsal
heads)

Metatarsal pads: off load metatarsal heads; placed posterior to the area of high stress or
force.
Forefoot posting
Medial: accommodates forefoot varus (supination), which is present in pes planovalgus

Lateral: accommodates plantarflexed first ray, which may drive the hindfoot into varus
Hindfoot posting
Medial: supports medial aspect of heel; corrects flexible valgus hindfoot alignment.
Lateral: supports lateral aspect of heel; corrects flexible varus hindfoot alignment.
Recessed first ray
Off-loads plantarflexed ray in cavovarus foot deformity

Placed beneath orthosis to stiffen entire foot (management of midfoot arthritis)

Examples of orthotic prescriptions
Pes planovalgus: full-length semi-rigid orthosis with medial heel posting, medial arch
support, and medial forefoot posting
Goal: more rigid support and hindfoot control
Pes cavovarus: full-length semirigid orthosis with lateral heel posting, recessed first ray,

Goal: provide more cushioning and shock absorption

Foot Orthoses
Prescribing appropriate foot orthoses for various foot and ankle pathology is a critical
component of nonsurgical management in any orthopaedic practice. A close working
relationship with a pedorthist may help optimize the treatment of these patients. In
general, most patients without major deformity or neuropathy can be treated via off-the-
shelf, prefabricated orthoses. In patients at risk for ulceration or in those who require
more complex off-loading or realignment, custom orthoses often are required. The two
main goals of in-shoe orthoses are to reduce force (pressure and friction) delivered to
the foot and help support or correct alignment problems.
Purely accommodative or rigid orthoses can be used; however, they do not have the
modularity and multilayered construction of a semi-rigid orthosis. Because semi-rigid
orthoses combine the soft cushioning and pressure relief of an accommodative orthosis
and the support and control of a rigid orthosis, semi-rigid orthoses are the most
commonly prescribed orthotic design.
Custom molded orthoses are fabricated by making a plaster mold (foam box or plaster
cast) of the foot or by developing a computer model of the foot via 3D scanning. This
process may be extremely time intensive and expensive and is not covered by most
insurance plans. An experienced pedorthist can use a combination of materials to meet
the specific requirements of the prescription. Newer computer-based processes may
reduce production time but may require more expensive machinery and 3D printers.

The top layer of the orthosis, which is in direct contact with the plantar skin, should be
composed of soft, moldable materials. Options include cross-linked polyethylene foams
(heat moldable but compress and lose thickness quickly), open-cell polyurethane foams
(reduce shear and absorb shock), and sponge rubber (maintain shape and thickness).
Additional layers of more supportive materials, including ethylene vinyl acetates, carbon
fiber, and cork composites, are used to provide the shape and support for the base of
the foot orthosis. This multilayer approach is crucial for total contact diabetic orthoses to
reduce plantar pressure, off-load bony deformities, and help control and support
malalignment of the foot and ankle.
Similar to shoes, foot orthoses can be modified to meet the various needs of a patient. A
carbon fiber plate or a Morton extension beneath the first ray can be used to stiffen the
shoe or to relieve pain from midfoot arthritis or hallux rigidus, respectively. Metatarsal
pads can be incorporated to relieve pressure on the metatarsal heads or from a Morton
neuroma. Forefoot and hindfoot posting can be used to help correct flexible deformities.
Lateral foot or heel posting is used for varus feet, whereas medial foot or heel posting is
used for valgus feet. If a varus deformity corrects with the Coleman block test, a
recessed first ray will off load the plantar flexed ray. For rigid deformities, such as stage
III pes planovalgus or tarsal coalitions, orthoses can only accommodate, not correct,
these alignment problems3 (Figure 4).

Articulated AFO
Foot and leg segments are connected by an articulating

Completely encloses the foot, ankle, and lower leg; maximizes

Double upright AFO

Carbon fiber AFO
Many of the same designs and functions as plastic AFOs; carbon
decreases bulk and returns recoil energy to the patient during

Post
Wedge under the medial or lateral forefoot to bring the floor up
to a varus or valgus deformity or used in the hindfoot medially

Cutout

area
Lift
Generally used as a neutral heel wedge to lift the heel and relax
the Achilles tendon
Cushion
Foam or other soft material used plantarly to relieve plantar
pressure
Extension
Rigid lengthening of the sole to the tips of the toes to reduce
bending forces of the midfoot and forefoot
Flange
Semirigid rim or lip extension on the orthosis to help support a
certain area, such as a collapsed arch
Metatarsal bar
Pad placed proximal to the metatarsal heads to unload plantar

Tall versus short walking boot8
Tall and short walking boots restrict range of motion of the talocrural and subtalar joints.
Tall walking boots reduce talocrural motion by 87% and subtalar motion by 37%.
Short walking boots reduce talocrural motion by 52% and subtalar motion by 26%.
A patient-specific approach should be used in deciding between a tall or short walking
boot.
Although many patients find a short walking boot more convenient, it may not be
adequate for immobilization for certain treatment options, such as ankle fracture or
subtalar fusion immobilization.

Lower Extremity Bracing
In considering lower extremity bracing, various off-the-shelf braces are suitable for
common foot and ankle conditions, including lateral ankle instability and posterior tibial
tendon dysfunction. In contrast to most ankle braces, which are designed to prevent
inversion injuries, the Airlift Posterior Tibial Tendon Dysfunction Brace (DJO Global) is
designed to lift the medial arch and off-load the posterior tibial tendon. A pneumatic
bladder and adjustable straps make this a good option for the initial management of
posterior tibial tendon dysfunction. Many other conditions, including Achilles
tendinopathy or substantial ligament injuries, initially are best managed with the use of a
fixed ankle walker (walking boot). Pneumatic walking boots may provide a more
adjustable fit and force distribution to the lower leg. Prolonged use of a fixed ankle
walker may result in proximal joint and back pain related to the effective leg-length
discrepancy. An elevated shoe or EVENup shoe leveler on the contralateral foot may
alleviate some of these effects (Figure 14)

For custom bracing options, the prescribing physician must consider whether the brace
is intended to eliminate or maintain joint motion. For example, a solid ankle AFO helps
prevent painful ankle motion in patients with advanced ankle arthritis. Conversely, a
hinged AFO can help control hindfoot deformity while permitting ankle range of motion
if the tibiotalar joint is preserved. Elastic or spring-loaded hinges can be incorporated to
compensate for loss of motor function from tendon rupture or nerve injury or palsy.
Molded gauntlet style braces, such as the Arizona brace, can control the foot and ankle
in all planes but may be bulky and difficult to fit into off-the-shelf shoes. They also can be
used to simulate an arthrodesis procedure and often are the last bracing option before
surgical management is considered. An Arizona Closed Toe Walker, a gauntlet brace
incorporated into a custom walking boot, may improve patient compliance and ease of
use because it obviates the need for an extra-wide or deep toe box shoe to
accommodate a gauntlet brace.

Incorporating metal struts into an off-the-shelf or custom shoe may off load the foot and
ankle substantially and may better accommodate substantial swelling that may prevent
the use of a solid ankle or circumferential brace. These double upright braces also may
incorporate straps or patellar tendon bearing components to provide additional control
or improve off-loading capacity. The modularity of this brace also allows shoes and
inserts to be replaced to account for changes in alignment or the progression of
deformities.
The Intrepid Dynamic Exoskeletal Orthosis(TechLink) uses a proximal cuff and carbon
fiber struts and foot plate to store and deliver kinetic energy and simulate dynamic ankle
motor function. This brace is a great option for extremely active patients who lack motor
function, have undergone arthrodesis procedures, or have substantial joint arthritis or
deformity.10
For patients with diabetes mellitus and severe Charcot degeneration, a Charcot Restraint
Orthotic Walker can maintain ambulatory status despite substantial collapse or rocker-
bottom deformity. The complete enclosure and modularity of the foot liner/orthosis
provide maximal protection and shock absorption for these high-risk patients. A recent
article reported that similar results can be attained with the use of an off-the-shelf
pneumatic walking boot plus custom total contact inserts.9
